analysis.one_liner: Cuts short layered drug patents so cheaper generic and biosimilar copies reach the market sooner.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee with zero cosponsors and died there when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name drug companies often file many patents on the same medicine — on small tweaks to the drug, its dosage, or its delivery — so that when the first patent expires, later patents keep cheaper generic copies off the market for years. This bill would change patent law so that, once the first patent on a drug expires, the later patents on that same drug are presumed to expire with it, unless the company proves each one covers a genuinely different invention. It would also direct the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office to review its own procedures for granting overlapping drug patents and report to Congress within a year.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and families who pay for prescription drugs, insurers and employers who cover them, and government programs like Medicare and Medicaid, all of whom would see cheaper generic and biosimilar versions of medicines reach the market sooner. Generic and biosimilar manufacturers also gain, since the patents used to block them would expire earlier.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a rule to patent law that once the first patent on a drug expires, the term of every later patent on that same drug is presumed to end too, cutting off the practice of stacking patents to extend a monopoly. [S2]
A company can escape the presumption only by proving, by a preponderance of the evidence, that its later patents cover patentably distinct inventions from the original drug. [S2]
The presumption applies in the legal proceedings where generic and biosimilar makers challenge drug patents, as well as in federal court cases involving those patents. [S2]

The bill directs the Patent Office to review whether its examination procedures are preventing improper issuance of overlapping drug patents that improperly extend a drug's exclusivity, and to report findings and recommendations to the House Judiciary Committee within one year. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies, which would lose some of the extra years of market exclusivity they currently get from filing multiple patents on the same drug. Their revenue from extended monopoly periods — which comes from patients, insurers, and government health programs paying higher prices — would shrink.

drawbacks.text: The rule is a presumption, not an absolute ban: a drug company can keep its later patent terms in full by showing its patents cover patentably distinct inventions, so the bill only raises the bar for patent stacking rather than eliminating it. [S2]

Stronger challenges to later patents could also make it harder to protect genuinely improved versions of a drug — such as a new formulation that is easier for patients to take — potentially reducing some incentives to invest in real improvements. [S2]
The Patent Office review is only a study with recommendations to one committee; it would not itself change examination practice without further action by Congress or the agency. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit for people who buy or insure prescription drugs is real: shorter monopolies mean generic competition arrives sooner and prices fall. But the bill's design is narrow — it works through a rebuttable presumption in specific patent-litigation settings, and companies skilled at demonstrating 'distinct inventions' could preserve much of their patent stacking. It is a targeted fix to one mechanism of extended drug exclusivity, not a sweeping reform.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Patrick Ryan introduced the bill in the House on November 15, 2023. [S1]
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary — the committee with jurisdiction over patent law. [S4]
No other action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action. [S4]
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor. [S3]
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired without ever receiving a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies came out ahead: the layered-patent strategy the bill targeted remains fully available, so the extended market exclusivity — and the higher prices that come with it — continues for drug makers, while patients keep paying.

for.name: Rep. Patrick Ryan
for.role: U.S. Representative, New York; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor; no other member cosponsored it.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over patent law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it; no roll-call vote was ever held.

industries.note: The bill would presume that later patents on the same drug expire with the first, cutting off a common strategy for extending monopolies beyond the original patent term. Shorter exclusivity means lower prices for patients and government health programs, and less monopoly revenue for the companies.

With fewer stacked patents blocking them, generic and biosimilar makers could launch copies of medicines sooner, which is how drug prices typically fall. Their interest runs directly alongside patients' interest in lower prices.
